This is by far my favorite potatoe side dish. I learned it from atleast a 3rd generation farm boy. Reason being is that I love a home cooked breakfast more than any other meal and the plate better have potatoes on it. Potatoe included in my breakfast is not only taste and nutritious, it also helps hold the rest of the meal in belly for better benifits of digestion. It is also known to, uh, make the day more productive, less break times if you know what I mean.. OK on with the show.

Here goes, you can do this recipe one at a time or prepare in advance for the whole week!! Store covered in the fridge. First decide how many you need, I'll have about 1 potatoe a day and maybe take 2 days off so, 5 potatoes. Peel them and cube them into bit sized or double bite sized for country style (big and hearty).

Next get a pot that they all fit in and you'll want a fait amount of water over the top of the taters. The water will be removing some of the starch, (this is good for the frying step so you don't have that gooey texture on the outside and desired results of crispy golden brown). Alrighty we have a pot of water heating to a boil, when it boils you can add the taters. We want a good boil but not a violent boil or a very light boil. The times will be different due to addition of salt if chosen for the boil and altitude and pot size. The goal here ultimately is a Par Boil. Think half way cooked. They should take a fork poke but not break apart. Check often enough as to not screw it up or you be having mashed potaoes all week. To halt the cooking process, dump into a colander and lighty wrinse with cold water. Give the pot a quick clean out now too. (If that's your storage vessel). Store well drained taters in cover container for up to a week. These are not raw anymore so water bath to stop oxidation is not needed.

Now they are ready to fry just like the store bought versions. Keep in mind if your using the ones from the fridge vs just par cooked they will be colder and will requirejust little bit more time. Decide how many servings and let er rip. I find this type of tater is best friend in Real Butter. Margarine and cooking oils just don't give a bold enough flavor for me, it can be done though if your diet demands it. Alrighty, get a pan pre heating on medium heat with a good chuck of butter, once it melts add taters, also add sliced onion, bell pepper, or what ever else you like, but I like the basics. This takes a fair amount of time compared to shedded hashbrowns, be patient and don't flip to early. It's time to rotate when they look almost done one side. I just shake them in the pan and toss to rotate. No lids, we don't want any water entering the pan. When they are golden brown all around and nicely fork tender they are done. You can make bacon in the pan first and remove most of the grease for bacon flavored and then when are about done add bacon back in heat it back up. Sausage links are another before and after meat option. They wen up in price last year because Walmart decided to sell a generic brand for the old price. Anyways Johnsonville links are $2.50 east of the Mississippi. Best link I can find that is available everywhere. In the ending minutes of frying I'll season with salt and freshly black pepper. Aim for under seasoning because it can fixed at the table.

I'll side these fried taters, next to two eggs up, a piece of Italian white bread toasted and buttered, and a breakfast meat if not included in the taters, (bacon, ham, sausages, and rarely a nice thin steak).
